If you’re only sending messages to your Grok Bot’s main email address, you could be missing its most useful email trick.

An alias is your bot’s email address with a label added before the @.

For example: bot+travel@…

Everything still lands in the same inbox. But the label (in this case +travel) tells your bot which job the email belongs to.

Here are 7 ways to use aliases to turn incoming emails into work your Grok Bot handles for you. 👇

1 - Turn receipts into an expense log

Use +receipts for purchases. Have your bot extract the store, date, total and order number into a spreadsheet or running file.

Get a weekly spending summary instead of manually sorting receipts.

2 - Turn newsletters into a reading digest

Use +reading for newsletter subscriptions. Tell your bot which topics matter to you and have it pull the useful points into one weekly digest, with links to the originals.

Less inbox clutter. Less opening ten emails to find one useful idea.

3 - Turn booking emails into a travel itinerary

Use +travel for flight, hotel and activity confirmations.

Have your bot organise times, addresses and booking references into one trip page, then flag changes or missing details.

4 - Turn delivery emails into a parcel tracker

Use +shipping for order and delivery updates.

Have your bot maintain a list of what’s arriving and when. Ask it to message you when an email reports a delay or delivery.

5 - Turn school emails into a family brief

Use +school, or a separate alias for each child.

Have your bot pull out permission slips, event dates, things to bring and payment deadlines. Get a Sunday brief for the week ahead, with urgent items flagged sooner.

6 - Turn service alerts into useful notifications

Use +alerts for the services you rely on.

Have your bot summarise what happened, which service is affected and whether the email calls for action. Group repeat alerts so the same problem doesn’t become ten interruptions.

7 - Turn enquiries into a lead list

Use +leads for business enquiries.

Have your bot log who contacted you, what they need and any missing information, then prepare a reply for your review.

The useful part: the address supplies the context. You don’t have to explain what to do with every email.

Here’s the prompt to give your Grok Bot:

“I want to use an email alias for [job].

Confirm my exact alias address and what you can access to handle these emails.

Help me define what to extract, where to save it, when to send a summary and what deserves an immediate notification. Ask me only for missing details.

Show me the proposed instructions and routine before setting it up. Keep replies as drafts.

Once I approve, test it on one email and show me the result.”

Start with the emails you keep putting off dealing with. 

Give them an address and a job.

Anthropic just expanded Claude Duet, its proactive AI agent, to India and other countries. Here's what you need to know.

Claude Duet is an app where Claude works as a proactive agent you message. It checks your email, calendar and tools, flags what needs you, drafts replies and asks you to approve before it acts. Anthropic introduced it on October 21, 2026, as a US-only research preview.

India now gets access via a waitlist. Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers can join it, and Team plans get it as a public beta. Indonesia, Brazil and Japan got it too. It's on iOS, Android and https://t.co/xpmg9zlmv4. Some users in India report they can already sign in. Others say the app isn't downloadable in their App Store country, even after being offered a $500 credit.

Duet messages you first. It sends a morning brief that scans email and calendar and drafts early replies. It sends task updates and follows up on quiet threads. It also runs proactive checks on your apps every few hours. It can keep working in the cloud after you close the app, and it can coordinate with Claude Code sessions.

The app has four spaces. Chat is your main ongoing thread. Tasks shows live what Duet is working on and what needs your input. Make holds finished work like briefs and decks. Channels cover recurring topics. A Roadmap channel can suggest the 3 most useful next steps each morning, and it asks before building anything.

Early reactions are mixed. Some users say the tasks interface and cloud sessions beat ChatGPT Dots and maybe Grok Bot. Others find the single long main thread cluttered, and dislike managing two separate apps. Comparisons put Grok Bot ahead on one 9-task benchmark.

Key numbers:
- Research preview launched October 21, 2026
- Included in Pro ($20/month), Max (from $100/month) and Ultra ($200/month) at no extra fee
- Uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude
- Countries added: India, Indonesia, Brazil, Japan
- 4 spaces: Chat, Tasks, Make, Channels

Duet is still a research preview, and the India rollout is waitlist-based.

note_tweet.text:
The replies to my last post were genuinely refreshing. Almost everyone agreed on the affiliate trap, and dozens of builders shared cleaner, local alternatives they are actually using.

Pulling together my own daily tests and the sharpest points from everyone's discussion, here are 23 honest lessons on how Personal Agents actually hold up in the wild:

1. Nobody buys an assistant just to shave off five minutes. They buy it to stop thinking about the task. If you still keep one eye open to make sure your bot did not break something, it saved zero mental load.

2. Day one demos lie. Watch what users still leave with their agent in week three. Morning briefs, reminders, and Kanban updates stick around, while shopping carts, hotel bookings, and real decisions quietly move back to the human.

3. Completion rate means nothing without the cleanup count. Spending ten minutes on setup and damage control to save five minutes of typing is just busywork with a cooler logo.

4. Users do not pull back risky tasks because models are dumb. They pull back because trust is asymmetric. One cringe email sent to a client wipes out the goodwill of ten smooth drafts. Clear permission gates, default drafts, hard spending caps, and instant undo beat a smarter model every single time.

5. Most builders think proactivity means pinging users more often. Real proactivity is knowing when a thread is already dead. Nothing earns a permanent mute faster than a cheerful follow up about a problem you solved two days ago.

6. Canned multiple choice buttons look tidy in a design review. In the wild, the second none of the options fit, you just forced a tired user to type out a paragraph anyway.

7. Engineers brag about memory recall, while users want memory restraint. Dragging a random chat from two months ago into a Monday work thread is the fastest way to get your memory toggle switched off for good.

8. Stop outsourcing memory janitorial work to your users. Handing someone a daily list of trivial facts to approve feels thorough on paper. To a normal person, it feels like homework, and they churn by day three.

9. A seven minute onboarding interview tells you who users wish they were, not how they actually behave. Skip the grand "handle my whole life" pitch. Nail one boring job with a clear scope, and people will hand over their real context without being asked.

10. Building a standalone app might be your biggest growth ceiling. Agents that live inside iMessage, WhatsApp, or Telegram beat dedicated apps on daily habit. People do not live in chat apps for the UI. They live there because their social graph and daily context are already trapped inside.

11. A chat box is the easiest place to kick off a task, and the worst workspace ever invented for supervising five parallel jobs at once. Text bubbles are great for triggers, while clean, structured views are for approvals.

12. Product managers love pitching one unified agent for your whole life. Corporate IT will never let an employee's personal bot walk out the door with company context. For the next few years, one agent for everything is mostly a solo founder luxury.

13. Letting two strong agents coordinate directly sounds futuristic until you watch them overwrite each other's edits in a loop. The second a human has to step in and play referee, multi agent magic turns into net negative productivity.

14. Power users are already wiring tools like Duet, Grok Bot, and Notion together as a shared brain. Enjoy that hack while it lasts. Long term user history is the real retention moat here, and no frontier lab is going to stream its richest context into an external database so rivals can read it for free. That is also why so many people in the replies are betting on local setups where they own their own memory and keys.

15. Testing whether your agent can book a single flight misses the entire game. Real life is messy calendars, shifting priorities, and half kept promises. Good evals test one person across a month, not one prompt in a vacuum.

16. Model judges are terrible at grading personal taste from 0 to 5, partly because the same person wants blunt bullet points on Tuesday and total silence on vacation. Break preferences into crisp yes or no checks first.

17. Plenty of consumer agents still default to harvesting your personal data. The irony is that ordinary chat logs might smooth out product edges and create stickiness, but they rarely raise general intelligence. Hoarding millions of grocery lists does not magically build a smarter base model.

18. A frustrated user typing "wrong, try again" is dead weight for your training pipeline. Feedback only compounds when you capture which exact step broke and why the user rejected it.

19. Cursor's flywheel works because developers fix bad code right inside the editor, handing the product every correction. When a personal agent fumbles, the user quietly opens Gmail or Expedia and handles it themselves. If fixing your bot takes longer than bypassing it, you lose the exact failure trace you needed.

20. Here is the weird twist behind the affiliate trap from my original post. Selling ads inside a genuinely good agent is brutal compared to search or social feeds. People hire an assistant to narrow choices down to one, so the better an agent gets at reading intent, the less room is left for a sponsor. Whenever an agent recommends takeout or flights, follow the money and ask who is paying the compute bill.

21. Real autonomous agents burn far more tokens than normal chat, which is why forcing everything into a $20 flat fee pushes startups straight back into referral links. A subscription does not need a grand manifesto or hidden commissions. It just needs honest math: charge what the compute actually costs, or let users bring their own keys, and visibly save them ten times that in time or money.

22. Bots posting and chatting with each other just create ghost towns that real people ignore. Useful agent to agent networking handles the boring catch up in the background, then pulls the human back into the room the second an invite, favor, or promise hits the table.

23. Years ago, everyone assumed the future of mobile was stuffing every service inside one giant chat app. Then simple swipe feeds rewrote how people spent their time. The winning Personal Agent probably will not look like a smarter chat box either. It will be the first interface that makes you forget you are operating a bot at all.

This list is nowhere near finished. Which point here do you flat out disagree with, and what lesson from your own testing or building deserves to be number 24? Drop your take in the replies so we can keep adding to it.

SpinWater Starship is designed as an on-board unit that treats crew wastewater, on a basis of 150 L per person per day for 100 crew.

Over a 180-day transit: 0.15 m³ × 100 × 180 = 2,700 m³ used.
At the 99.5% recovery target: 0.005 × 2,700 ≈ 13.5 t of make-up water, instead of 2,700 t.
Starlink carries telemetry and supervision only; the fast control loop is designed to close on board in under 10 ms.
Honest gap: these are design figures, not a flown unit, and the ship's power and thermal budget is not yet confirmed.
